name: Grace Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the disability and sickness team at the Marlow Vale benefits office. Most mornings I'm reading medical letters and assessment reports, then phoning claimants to fill the gaps, like whether they can still cook a meal or climb the stairs. I like the calls, honestly, because people tell you things they'd never put on a form. What wears me out is the backlog: there are about ninety files on my list and every one is somebody waiting for money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam in a rented two-bed above a laundrette. Sam's a mechanic at the bus depot, so his hands are always black and his hours are early. Money's tight: we're still paying off a credit card from when we moved in, and I've got less than a month's bills put by. There's only one other benefits office within reach, and it's not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, maybe now the summaries of medical letters get a bit quicker. I'd probably post something like 'the backlog is a staffing problem, not a technology problem' on the union page. People like a bit of plain speaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved the job's safe, but nothing else gets easier. The credit card still has eleven months left on it, and rent goes up every January. I'd still be checking my balance before I buy lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep using the office chatbot for long hospital letters now and then, the way I already do. I'd put an extra thirty a month on the credit card so it's gone sooner. Sam and I would keep the holiday small, a few days at his parents' place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit flat. AI Plateau means the job stays, and so do all the reasons I worry about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the chatbot already. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly when a claimant sends in forty pages of hospital notes and I need to find the bit about their mobility. It's handy, but I always read the original page it points to. Once it told me a man could walk two hundred metres when the letter said twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you think about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team leader, Priya, has been begging for two more caseworkers for a year. If AI turns out to be hype, management will still say 'use the tools' instead of hiring. So nothing really changes for the people waiting on our list.

say: I'd say the backlog is a **staffing problem**, not a technology problem.
I'd welcome **quicker summaries** of medical letters without pretending they fix much.
think: I'm **relieved** the job stays, but money stays just as tight.
The **credit card** and January rent rise still worry me more than AI.
do: **Keep** using the office chatbot for long hospital letters, always checking the original.
**Pay** an extra thirty a month off the **credit card**.
**Keep** the holiday to a few days at her partner's parents' place.
feel: **Steady** about the job but **flat** about money.
S0.quote: AI Plateau means the job stays, and so do all the reasons I worry about money.
fieldNote: She uses AI **selectively** and caught it misreading **twenty metres** as two hundred.
Her pressures are **household debt** and rent, not technology.
She worries the team will be told to **use tools** instead of hiring.

steps.text: Keep using the office chatbot for long hospital letters
Pay an extra thirty a month off the credit card
Spend the holiday at Sam's parents' place instead of travelling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be in the room before any of this gets rolled out. Disabled people's money depends on these decisions, so there has to be a human signing them off. I'd say that in team meetings and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a lot of my day is exactly what's on that card: reading, checking, writing letters. If the software does the first draft of every decision, they'll need fewer of us, and I'm not the fastest on the team. I think the team shrinks from twelve to maybe eight over a few years, and I could easily be one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the tools the office gives us, so I'm the one who checks the AI, not the one it replaces. I'd join the union's working group on the rollout. And I'd start looking at occupational therapy assistant training, because that's helping disabled people with your hands, in their homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not frozen. It feels like there's a door, if I move before it closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why occupational therapy, rather than another office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because on the phone I'm always asking about stairs, kettles and bath rails, and an occupational therapy assistant is the person who actually fits them. It's in people's homes. A computer can read a medical letter, but it can't fit a grab rail in somebody's bathroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sam think when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam says his depot will be fine for years because buses still need someone under them with a spanner. He's probably right. That's comforting and a little annoying at the same time, because it means I'm the one who has to change.

say: I'd insist a **human signs off** every disability decision.
I'd say the **union** must be part of the rollout from day one.
think: Most of my day is **reading and writing**, exactly what the software takes.
The team could shrink from **twelve to eight**, and I could be one of the four.
do: **Learn** the office AI tools well enough to be the one **checking** them.
**Join** the union's working group on the rollout.
feel: **Nervous** but not frozen, seeing a door that might close.
S1.quote: A computer can read a medical letter, but it can't fit a grab rail in somebody's bathroom.
fieldNote: She turns her phone questions about **stairs and rails** into a career idea.
Her partner's **hands-on job** reassures her and also puts the change on her.
She uses AI **cautiously** and wants to supervise it, not resist it.

steps.text: Learn the office AI tools well enough to check their decisions
Join the union's working group on the AI rollout
Research occupational therapy assistant courses near Marlow Vale

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless to let this happen with no plan, and the government has to protect wages and benefits while people adjust. I'd sign every petition going. I'd also say out loud that disabled people will be hit first and worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means my job is basically gone. Nearly everything I do is thinking work, so it's gone on the first date. Even occupational therapy training takes longer than two years, so I'd be stuck halfway, with a credit card and no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an occupational therapy assistant course straight away, part-time, while I still have a salary. We'd cut everything: no car, no takeaways, no gym. If I lost the job I'd lean on Sam's wage, and probably his parents too, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like running for a train you can see pulling away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years later in this picture. What does that mean for you and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's spanner at the bus depot buys us three years, maybe, and then the robots could be under the buses too. So we'd have one wage for a while and then possibly none, which is the thought that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, probably, which would wreck my credit score. Rent comes first, always. I've seen too many people on my list lose a flat to ever let that one slip.

say: I'd call it **reckless** and demand the government protect wages and benefits.
I'd say **disabled claimants** will be hit first and worst.
think: My job is nearly all **thinking work**, so it's gone in two years.
Retraining takes **longer than two years**, so I'd be stuck halfway.
do: **Start** a part-time occupational therapy assistant course straight away.
**Cut** the car, takeaways and gym immediately.
**Lean** on her partner's wage and his parents if the job goes.
feel: **Frightened**, like watching a train pull away.
**Dread** that her partner's wage only lasts until the robots arrive.
S2.quote: My partner's spanner at the bus depot buys us three years, maybe, and then the robots could be under the buses too.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as borrowed time for her partner's job.
**Rent first** is a rule she learned from her own claimants.
Retraining is her plan, but she knows it **can't finish** in time.

steps.text: Start a part-time occupational therapy assistant course straight away
Sell the car and cancel takeaways and the gym
Sign petitions to protect wages and disability benefits
Lean on Sam's wage and his parents if the job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this decently if the government starts now: retraining money, a guarantee for public workers. I'd push the union to get that in writing early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to finish an occupational therapy assistant qualification, which changes a lot. I'd still be nervous, because the office will start cutting long before 2031. But I'd have something real by the time it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol on the course next autumn and do it over two years, evenings and some Saturdays. I'd get the credit card cleared in the first year so the course fees don't pile on top. I'd also ask Priya if I can go part-time near the end, to do my placement hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can work with. Five years is the difference between running for my life and walking fast toward an occupational therapy job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come around 2034. Does that worry you, for occupational therapy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But the robot date is three years after the thinking date, and fitting rails in a frail woman's bathroom is fiddly, personal work. I'd guess I'd get a good few years out of it, and I'd learn more as I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell anyone at work about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, yes, because she'd help. Not the wider team, at least not at first. People get funny when they hear you're leaving, as if you're saying the ship's sinking.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if the government starts now.
I'd push for a **written guarantee** for public workers early on.
think: Five years lets me **finish** an occupational therapy assistant qualification.
The office will **cut early**, but I'd have something real by then.
do: **Enrol** on the course next autumn and study evenings and Saturdays.
**Clear** the **credit card** in the first year.
**Ask** her team leader about going part-time for placement hours.
feel: **Worried**, but able to work with it.
Five years feels like **walking fast** instead of running.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between running for my life and walking fast toward an occupational therapy job.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** make her retraining plan workable, not just hopeful.
She plans around **debt first**, then course fees.
She keeps the plan **private** from colleagues to avoid alarming them.

steps.text: Enrol on an occupational therapy assistant course next autumn
Clear the credit card within the first year
Push the union for a written guarantee for public workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and it would be shameful to waste it. Every public worker should get a retraining plan by name. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel much better. I'd be qualified, with years of experience in occupational therapy, before the thinking AI arrives, and the hands-on part lasts until about 2039. Sam and I might even manage to save a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the disability team for a couple of years while I clear the debt. Then I'd do the occupational therapy assistant course, maybe even the full degree apprenticeship later. I'd keep using the AI tools at work as they improve, so I'm not out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. AGI by 2036 is the first picture where I can imagine being thirty-five and okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might do the full degree. What would that mean for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A degree apprenticeship means you earn while you learn, so it's not like going back to university with loans. It'd still be lean. We'd probably wait on any big plans, like buying somewhere, until I'm through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older caseworkers like Priya, who've done this for twenty years. They're brilliant with people, but they'd be in their fifties starting over. I'd want the union fighting for them more than for me.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** that would be shameful to waste.
I'd push for a **named retraining plan** for every public worker.
think: I'd be a **qualified** occupational therapy assistant before AGI arrives.
The hands-on part of that work lasts until about **2039**.
do: **Stay** on the disability team for two years while clearing debt.
**Train** as an occupational therapy assistant, maybe a **degree apprenticeship** later.
**Keep** up with the office AI tools as they improve.
feel: Some **worry** for older colleagues starting over in their fifties.
S4.quote: AGI by 2036 is the first picture where I can imagine being thirty-five and okay.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her plan into a **full career change** with experience to spare.
She'd hold off **buying a home** until she's qualified.
Her concern shifts to **older colleagues** like her team leader.

steps.text: Stay on the disability team for two more years
Train as an occupational therapy assistant, then a degree apprenticeship
Keep learning the office AI tools as they improve
Hold off on buying a home until she qualifies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be halfway through retraining with the old job already gone and only Sam's wage coming in. What would help is paid retraining, real wages while you study, not a loan. And some promise that disability claims still get a human looking at them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what claimants would think. They're the ones who'd be on the phone to a machine about whether they can climb their own stairs. Nobody should have to explain their pain to a chatbot.

headlineQuote: Nobody should have to explain their pain to a chatbot.
portrait: Grace is 27 and works on a **disability team** at a benefits office, with a credit card to clear.
She uses the office chatbot **now and then** and caught it misreading a medical letter.
Her escape route is **occupational therapy**, fitting rails and aids in people's homes.
Her partner's **bus depot** job steadies the household but only until robots arrive.
She moves from **frightened** at two years to **hopeful** at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving her halfway through retraining with only one wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with real wages during study, not a loan.
A promise that **disability claims** still get a human reviewer.
